products.name: pg-boss
products.summary: pg-boss is a job queue for Node.js built on PostgreSQL, with workers that claim jobs with SKIP LOCKED.

transactional-enqueue.note: Pass a db option to send(). Adapters exist for Knex, Kysely, Drizzle, and Prisma.
transactional-enqueue.evidence: Jobs can be part of your own transactions. ... you can send one in the same transaction as the data change it belongs to: the job exists if, and only if, the change commits.

scheduled-enqueue.evidence: Deferred jobs: startAfter int, string, or Date. int: seconds to delay starting the job; string: Start after an ISO 8601 date time string, or after a relative interval; Date: Start after a Date object

recurring-schedules.note: Cron and RRULE schedules. Precision is one minute.
recurring-schedules.evidence: Jobs may be created automatically based on a cron expression or an RRULE. ... schedules are checked every 30 seconds ... A schedule therefore sends at most one job a minute

priorities.evidence: priority, int: optional priority. Higher numbers have, um, higher priority. (fetch(): "Jobs are always fetched in priority order.")

enqueue-deduplication.note: Queue policies and singletonKey refuse duplicates. send() then resolves null. upsert() merges by key.
enqueue-deduplication.evidence: short: Only allows 1 job to be queued ... Can be extended with singletonKey | exclusive: Only allows 1 job to be queued or active. Can be extended with singletonKey

debounce-throttle.note: Throttle refuses a second job in a time slot. Debounce moves it to the next slot.
debounce-throttle.evidence: sendThrottled(name, data, options, seconds, key) ... sendDebounced(): Like sendThrottled(), but instead of rejecting if a job is already sent in the current interval, it will try to add the job to the next interval

task-dependencies.note: flow() creates jobs with dependsOn refs. A failed parent leaves the child blocked.
task-dependencies.evidence: flow(jobs, options): Create a set of jobs and their dependencies atomically in one transaction. ... Dependent jobs are created in a blocked state and won't be eligible for fetching until all parent jobs have completed.

retries.evidence: retryLimit, int Default: 2 ... retryDelay, int Default: 0. Delay between retries ... retryBackoff, bool ... Enables exponential backoff retries ... retryDelayMax

crash-recovery.note: Expiration retries a stuck job. An optional heartbeat detects a dead worker sooner.
crash-recovery.evidence: heartbeatSeconds ... If no heartbeat is received within this interval, the monitor will fail/retry the job. ... Expiration (expireInSeconds) is the maximum time a job is allowed to remain active.

cancellation.note: The handler gets job.signal on its next heartbeat. This needs heartbeatSeconds on the job.
cancellation.evidence: cancel(name, id, options): Cancels a pending or active job. (workers.md L270: signal "Aborted ... when a heartbeat finds this job no longer active under this worker's claim")

concurrency-limits.note: groupConcurrency limits each group key across all nodes. No setting limits a whole queue above one job. The docs say that a race can briefly exceed the limit.
concurrency-limits.evidence: groupConcurrency ... Limits how many jobs from the same group can be processed simultaneously globally across all nodes. ... there may be brief moments where the limit is slightly exceeded

rate-limits.note: Throttling limits job creation to one per time slot and key. No limit on start rate.
rate-limits.evidence: Throttling jobs to 'one per time slot'. This option is set on the send side of the API ... if you set the singletonSeconds to 60, then submit 2 jobs within the same minute, only the first job will be accepted

checkpoints.note: A retry runs the whole handler again. Flows split work into separate jobs.
checkpoints.evidence: Jobs are delivered at least once. If a worker crashes ... the job is retried, so a handler can run more than once for the same job. Write handlers so that running one twice does no harm. (No step API in docs/api.)

durable-waits.note: A running job cannot suspend. A flow child or a startAfter job waits before it starts.
durable-waits.evidence: Dependent jobs are created in a blocked state and won't be eligible for fetching until all parent jobs have completed. (Looked at docs/api: no API suspends a running job for a timer or signal.)

dashboard.note: Free, MIT. A separate package, @pg-boss/dashboard, in packages/dashboard of the same repository.
dashboard.evidence: A web-based dashboard is available in the @pg-boss/dashboard package for monitoring and managing jobs, queues and schedules. ... Job Actions: Create, cancel, retry, resume, or delete jobs directly from the UI

dead-letters.note: A dead letter queue keeps failed jobs, and redrive() creates them again.
dead-letters.evidence: redrive(name, options): Moves jobs out of a dead letter queue and re-creates them as fresh jobs on their original source queue. (retry(name, id) also retries a failed job.)

queue-pause.note: No queue pause. offWork() stops the workers of one process only.
queue-pause.evidence: updateQueue(name, options): Updates options on an existing queue ... (Looked at createQueue, updateQueue and the queue API: no pause option or method.) workers.md: "Workers can be stopped via offWork()"

opentelemetry.note: Core ships traces and metrics. Trace context propagation is opt-in through propagateContext.
opentelemetry.evidence: pg-boss creates OpenTelemetry spans and metrics following the messaging semantic conventions. It uses @opentelemetry/api, declared as a peer dependency

worker-languages.note: One Node.js library. It also runs on Bun.
worker-languages.evidence: Requirements: Node 22.12 or higher, or Bun; PostgreSQL 13 or higher

enqueue-languages.note: Other runtimes can call the HTTP proxy package or write SQL.
enqueue-languages.evidence: An HTTP proxy is available in the @pg-boss/proxy package, exposing pg-boss methods over a simple JSON API. It's useful for platform compatibility (calling pg-boss from non-Node runtimes or serverless functions)

infrastructure.note: CockroachDB, Citus, and PGlite are other backends.
infrastructure.evidence: Requirements: Node 22.12 or higher, or Bun; PostgreSQL 13 or higher

license.note: No paid edition. The dashboard and proxy packages are also MIT.
license.evidence: The MIT License (MIT) Copyright (c) 2016 Tim Jones

workhorse.note: A Worker handler commits its own writes. A TypeScript Queue from forTransaction can call complete in your transaction.

cell.note: The transactional option opens one transaction for handler writes and completion.
cell.evidence: transactional, bool: Run the handler and the job's completion inside one database transaction. ... Everything written through tx commits with the job's completion

rows.label: Databases other than PostgreSQL

workhorse.note: PostgreSQL only.

cell.note: The backend option selects CockroachDB, Citus, or in-process PGlite.
cell.evidence: pg-boss runs on stock single-node PostgreSQL by default, but it also supports several PostgreSQL-compatible backends. Those are distributed SQL engines like CockroachDB and Citus, plus the embedded WASM build PGlite.

products.name: Graphile Worker
products.summary: Graphile Worker is a job queue that uses PostgreSQL to store jobs and executes them on Node.js.

transactional-enqueue.note: add_job is a SQL function, so it runs in the caller's transaction.
transactional-enqueue.evidence: "You can schedule jobs directly in the database, e.g. from a trigger or function, or by calling SQL from your application code. You do this using the graphile_worker.add_job function"

scheduled-enqueue.evidence: run_at — a timestamp after which to run the job; defaults to now. (addJob: runAt, a Date to schedule this task to run in the future)

recurring-schedules.note: A crontab in UTC. It can backfill runs that it missed.
recurring-schedules.evidence: Graphile Worker supports triggering recurring tasks according to a cron-like schedule. ... can backfill missed jobs if desired ... works reliably even if you're running multiple workers (cron.md L37-L40: We only handle timestamps in UTC.)

priorities.evidence: priority — an integer representing the jobs priority. Jobs are executed in numerically ascending order of priority (jobs with a numerically smaller priority are run first). Defaults to 0.

enqueue-deduplication.note: The unsafe_dedupe mode keeps the first job. The default mode replaces a pending job with the same job_key.
enqueue-deduplication.evidence: unsafe_dedupe - if an existing job is found, even if it is locked or permanently failed, then it won't be updated. This is very dangerous ... (replace (default) - overwrites the unlocked job with the new values)

debounce-throttle.note: A job_key in replace mode debounces. In preserve_run_at mode it throttles.
debounce-throttle.evidence: replace (default) - ... primarily useful for rescheduling, updating, or debouncing ... preserve_run_at - ... primarily useful for throttling (executing at most once over a given time period)

task-dependencies.note: A task can add the next job itself.
task-dependencies.evidence: Reviewed the add_job parameters (identifier, payload, queue_name, run_at, max_attempts, job_key, priority, flags, job_key_mode) and the docs: no parameter makes a job wait for other jobs. (tasks.md: helpers.addJob())

retries.note: The backoff formula is fixed. The default is 25 attempts.
retries.evidence: We currently use the formula exp(least(10, attempt)) to determine the delays between attempts ... after ~4 hours attempts will be made every ~6 hours (sql-add-job.md L29: max_attempts defaults to 25)

crash-recovery.note: After a crash or SIGKILL, a job stays locked for at least 4 hours. The paid Worker Pro releases it sooner.
crash-recovery.evidence: the jobs that that worker was executing remain locked for at least 4 hours. Every 8-10 minutes a worker will sweep for jobs that have been locked for more than 4 hours and will make them available to be processed again automatically. (pro/recovery.md: Worker Pro tracks running workers via a heartbeat)

cancellation.note: Admin functions skip running jobs. helpers.abortSignal fires on shutdown.
cancellation.evidence: Unless otherwise noted, these functions ignore locked jobs (which includes all currently running jobs). (tasks.md L226-L233: abortSignal is triggered when the job should exit early ... for example, for a graceful shutdown request; marked Experimental)

concurrency-limits.note: A named queue runs one job at a time. A higher limit needs dedicated workers or several named queues.
concurrency-limits.evidence: Out of the box, Graphile Worker supports jobs being added to a named queue (in which case that queue has a concurrency of 1) ... Sometimes you want to limit concurrency to a small number, but larger than 1... Here are some techniques

rate-limits.note: No built-in limit for a queue or a key. forbiddenFlags lets the application skip jobs to build one.
rate-limits.evidence: graphile-worker will invoke it each time a worker looks for a job to run, and will skip over any job that has any flag returned by your function. ... For an example of how this can be used to achieve rate-limiting logic, see the graphile-worker-rate-limiter project (forbidden-flags.md L6-L9: jobs with any of the given flags should not be executed)

checkpoints.note: A retry runs the whole task again. The docs suggest smaller jobs instead.
checkpoints.evidence: Reviewed tasks.md and error-handling docs: no step API. "Graphile Worker automatically retries the job if it fails, so it's often sensible to split a large job into multiple smaller jobs"

durable-waits.note: A job waits only before it starts, through run_at.
durable-waits.evidence: Reviewed the task helpers (abortPromise, abortSignal, addJob, addJobs, getQueueName, job, logger, query, withPgClient) and the docs: no helper suspends a running job for a timer or a signal.

dashboard.note: No web UI ships. Admin functions help you build your own.
dashboard.evidence: "When implementing an administrative UI you may need more control over the jobs. For this we have added a few administrative functions that can be called in SQL or through the JS API." No UI package in the docs.

dead-letters.note: A job that uses all its attempts stays in the table. reschedule_jobs runs it again.
dead-letters.evidence: This method can be used to postpone or advance job execution, or to schedule a previously failed or permanently failed job for execution. (permanently_fail_jobs: setting their attempts equal to their max_attempts)

queue-pause.note: forbiddenFlags can hold back jobs that carry a flag.
queue-pause.evidence: Reviewed the admin functions (complete_jobs, permanently_fail_jobs, reschedule_jobs, force_unlock_workers, cleanup) and the config docs: no queue pause.

opentelemetry.note: Worker events and a custom logger can feed your own telemetry.
opentelemetry.evidence: Reviewed the docs, src, and package.json at v0.18.0: no OpenTelemetry dependency or integration. The events emitter reports worker and job events (worker-events.md L5-L10). library/logger.md L6-L10: You can override this by passing a custom logger.

worker-languages.note: Workers run on Node.js. An experimental loader runs executable files as tasks.
worker-languages.evidence: "if Graphile Worker finds an executable file inside of the taskDirectory it will create a task executor for it" (marked Experimental). Task executors are otherwise Node.js modules.

enqueue-languages.note: add_job is a SQL function. A database trigger can also call it.
enqueue-languages.evidence: You can schedule jobs directly in the database, e.g. from a trigger or function, or by calling SQL from your application code. You do this using the graphile_worker.add_job function

infrastructure.note: Workers run in Node.js processes beside the application.
infrastructure.evidence: "Graphile Worker is a job queue which uses PostgreSQL to store jobs, and executes them on Node.js."

license.note: Worker Pro is a paid proprietary preset for sponsors.
license.evidence: package.json: "license": "MIT". website/docs/pro/index.md#L6: "Worker Pro (@graphile-pro/worker) is a proprietary (not open source) preset"

rows.label: Process many items in one handler call

workhorse.note: Each task in a batch has its own outcome.

cell.note: One job holds an array payload. If the handler returns one promise for each item, a retry keeps only the items that failed.
cell.evidence: If the payload is an array, then optionally your task executor may choose to return an array of the same length, the entries in which are promises. Should any of these promises reject, then the job will be re-enqueued, but the payload will be overwritten to only contain the entries associated with the rejected promises

products.name: River
products.summary: River is a job processing system for Go and Postgres that encourages using the same database for application data and the job queue.

transactional-enqueue.note: Client.InsertTx inserts a job in the application's transaction.
transactional-enqueue.evidence: "Jobs are guaranteed to be enqueued if their transaction commits, are removed if their transaction rolls back, and aren't visible for work _until_ commit."

scheduled-enqueue.evidence: ScheduledAt is a time in future at which to schedule the job (i.e. in cases where it shouldn't be run immediately). The job is guaranteed not to run before this time

recurring-schedules.note: Intervals, or cron through a separate package. The elected leader keeps the schedule state in memory.
recurring-schedules.evidence: The helper PeriodicInterval is available for jobs that should run on simple, fixed intervals ... a custom schedule or third party cron package can be used ... each scheduler only retains in-memory state, so anytime a process quits or a new leader is elected, the whole process starts over

priorities.evidence: Priority is the priority of the job, with 1 being the highest priority and 4 being the lowest. When fetching available jobs to work, the highest priority jobs will always be fetched before any lower priority jobs

enqueue-deduplication.note: UniqueOpts refuses a duplicate by kind, args, period, queue, and state.
enqueue-deduplication.evidence: UniqueOpts contains parameters for uniqueness for a job. ... Uniqueness relies on a hash of the job kind and any unique properties along with a database unique constraint.

debounce-throttle.note: UniqueOpts with ByPeriod refuses a second job for each key in the period. No option gives debounce.
debounce-throttle.evidence: ByPeriod ... a job is only inserted if there isn't an existing job that will run between then and the next multiple of the period. The UniqueOpts fields (insert_opts.go#L102-L227) are ByArgs, ByPeriod, ByQueue, ByState, and ExcludeKind.

task-dependencies.note: Workflows with dependencies are in River Pro, the paid edition. The free library has none.
task-dependencies.evidence: type workflowTaskSerializable struct { ... Deps []string `json:"deps"`; IgnoreCancelledDeps ...; WorkflowID string } (riverproui, the River Pro build of River UI). No dependency option in insert_opts.go at v0.49.0.

retries.note: The default is 25 attempts with ATTEMPT^4 backoff. A worker can override NextRetry.
retries.evidence: DefaultClientRetryPolicy is River's default retry policy. ... Reschedules using a basic exponential backoff of `ATTEMPT^4` (client.go: MaxAttempts "defaults to 25")

crash-recovery.note: A rescuer retries a job that runs longer than RescueStuckJobsAfter. The default is one hour.
crash-recovery.evidence: RescueStuckJobsAfter is the amount of time a job can be running before it is considered stuck. ... This prevents jobs from being stuck forever if a worker crashes or is killed. ... this can result in repeat or duplicate execution of a job that is not actually stuck

cancellation.note: JobCancel cancels the context of the running job. Cancellation is cooperative.
cancellation.evidence: If the job is currently running, it is not immediately cancelled, but is instead marked for cancellation. The client running the job will also be notified to cancel the running job's context. ... it is important for workers to respect context cancellation

concurrency-limits.note: MaxWorkers limits each client process only. River Pro, a paid package, adds global limits and limits for each key.
concurrency-limits.evidence: This is the maximum number of workers within this particular client instance, but note that it doesn't control the total number of workers across parallel processes. River Pro: https://github.com/riverqueue/riverui/blob/v0.21.0/riverproui/internal/uitype/ui_api_types.go#L5-L13 defines ConcurrencyConfig with GlobalLimit, LocalLimit, and Partition.ByArgs.

rate-limits.note: QueueConfig has worker counts and fetch intervals only. No limit on start rate for a queue or a key.
rate-limits.evidence: type QueueConfig struct { FetchCooldown ...; FetchPollInterval ...; MaxWorkers int } (Looked at Config, QueueConfig, and InsertOpts: no option limits how many jobs start in a time period.)

checkpoints.note: ResumableStep skips completed steps on a retry. River records the last step when the attempt ends, or at once with ResumableSetStepTx. A step stores no result.
checkpoints.evidence: ResumableStep runs a resumable step, skipping the step on a later retry if an earlier attempt already completed it successfully. (resumable_step_tx.go#L19-L24: "Normally, a resumable job's step progress is recorded after it runs along with its result status. ... ResumableSetStepTx ... guarantee of a checkpoint being recorded durably")

durable-waits.note: JobSnooze frees the worker until a later time. River Pro, the paid edition, adds workflow signals and timers.
durable-waits.evidence: JobSnooze can be returned from a Worker's Work method to cause the job to be tried again after the specified duration. This will not increment the job's Attempt count. River Pro: https://github.com/riverqueue/riverui/blob/v0.21.0/CHANGELOG.md#L67 "the all new workflow engine in River Pro v0.24.0, including signals, timers"

dashboard.note: River UI is a free separate package. A riverproui build adds River Pro views.
dashboard.evidence: "River UI is a graphical user interface for the River job queue. It lets users view and manage jobs without having to resort to querying the database or the command line."

dead-letters.note: Discarded jobs stay for 7 days by default. JobRetry runs a job again.
dead-letters.evidence: JobRetry updates the job with the given ID to make it immediately available to be retried. ... MaxAttempts is also incremented by one if the job has already exhausted its max attempts. (client.go#L131-L137: DiscardedJobRetentionPeriod "Defaults to 7 days.")

queue-pause.evidence: QueuePause pauses the queue with the given name. When a queue is paused, clients will not fetch any more jobs for that particular queue. To pause all queues at once, use the special queue name "*".

opentelemetry.note: The otelriver middleware in the rivercontrib repository gives traces and metrics.
opentelemetry.evidence: OpenTelemetry utilities for the River job queue. ... otelriver.NewMiddleware(&MiddlewareConfig{ ... MeterProvider: meterProvider, TracerProvider: tracerProvider })

worker-languages.note: Go is the main SDK. The Ruby, Rust, and TypeScript SDKs are pre-1.0 and have their own tags.
worker-languages.evidence: js/v0.2.0: "shares River's database protocol with River for Go and Rust, so services in all three languages can insert and work the same jobs". ruby/v0.13.0 docs: "It inserts and works jobs".

enqueue-languages.note: The Python client inserts jobs only.
enqueue-languages.evidence: An insert-only Python client for River ... Allows jobs to be inserted in Python and run by a Go worker, but doesn't support working jobs in Python.

infrastructure.note: PostgreSQL is the main target. A SQLite driver ships in the same module.
infrastructure.evidence: doc.go: "robust high-performance job processing system for Go and Postgres". river_sqlite_driver.go: "Package riversqlite provides a River driver implementation for SQLite."

license.note: River Pro is a paid extension package.
license.evidence: LICENSE: "Mozilla Public License Version 2.0". riverqueue.com/pro: "Extend River with durable workflows, concurrency limits, sequences, and more."

workhorse.note: Up to 1,000 tasks commit or roll back together.

cell.note: InsertManyTx inserts the jobs in the application's transaction.
cell.evidence: InsertManyTx inserts many jobs at once. ... This variant lets a caller insert jobs atomically alongside other database changes.

products.name: Solid Queue
products.summary: Solid Queue is a database-based queuing backend for Active Job.

transactional-enqueue.note: Only when Solid Queue uses the app database. The default setup uses a separate one.
transactional-enqueue.evidence: "taking advantage of transactional integrity to ensure some action in your app is not committed unless your job is also committed and vice versa" ... "by default Solid Queue is configured in a different database as the main app."

scheduled-enqueue.evidence: Jobs set to run in the future (via Active Job's `wait` or `wait_until` options) have concurrency limits enforced when they're due, not when they're scheduled.

recurring-schedules.note: Cron schedules in config/recurring.yml, or tasks that the application adds at runtime.
recurring-schedules.evidence: Solid Queue supports defining recurring tasks that run at specific times in the future, on a regular basis like cron jobs. ... (L937: "You can schedule and unschedule recurring tasks at runtime, without editing the configuration file." L947: SolidQueue.schedule_recurring_task.)

priorities.note: A lower number runs first. The queue order of a worker comes before the priority.
priorities.evidence: In Solid Queue, the smaller the value, the higher the priority. The default is `0`. ... in a list of queues, the queue order takes precedence

enqueue-deduplication.note: With on_conflict: :discard, a concurrency control drops a new job while another job with the same key holds the limit.
enqueue-deduplication.evidence: Alternatively, jobs can be configured to be discarded instead of blocked. This means that if a job with certain arguments has already been enqueued, other jobs with the same characteristics (in the same concurrency class) won't be enqueued. ... `:discard`: the job is discarded.

debounce-throttle.note: limits_concurrency with on_conflict: :discard drops a job while another job with the same key runs. This has no time period, and no option gives debounce.
debounce-throttle.evidence: `:discard`: the job is discarded. ... This means that the `duration` is not really about the job that's enqueued or being run, it's about the jobs that are blocked waiting

task-dependencies.note: A batch starts a callback job when all its jobs finish. No API makes a job wait for jobs outside its batch.
task-dependencies.evidence: Solid Queue supports grouping jobs into batches ... `on_finish`: fired when all jobs have finished ... `on_success` ... `on_failure` (L744: "A job joins the batch that's active when its enqueue is requested". Looked at the README: no option makes a job start after a job outside its batch.)

retries.note: Active Job retry_on gives the retries and the backoff. Solid Queue has no retry of its own.
retries.evidence: Solid Queue doesn't include any automatic retry mechanism, it relies on Active Job for this. (Rails v8.1.4 exceptions.rb#L64: def retry_on(*exceptions, wait: 3.seconds, attempts: 5, ...), with wait: :polynomially_longer.)

crash-recovery.note: A graceful stop puts jobs back in the queue. If a worker process dies, its jobs fail and need a manual or a custom retry.
crash-recovery.evidence: Once another process notices the missing heartbeats and prunes the dead process's registration, its in-flight jobs are marked as failed with `SolidQueue::Processes::ProcessPrunedError`. Solid Queue deliberately doesn't retry these automatically (L402: on QUIT, in-flight jobs "will be returned to the queue")

cancellation.note: A job in progress cannot be discarded. Active Job has no cancel API.
cancellation.evidence: def discard; raise UndiscardableError, "Can't discard a job in progress"; end

concurrency-limits.note: limits_concurrency limits each key across all workers. No setting limits a whole queue. After the duration, another job can take the limit.
concurrency-limits.evidence: Solid Queue extends Active Job with concurrency controls, that allows you to limit how many jobs of a certain type or with certain arguments can run at the same time. ... we'll ensure that, at most, the number of jobs (indicated as `to`) that yield the same `key` will be performed concurrently, and this guarantee will last for `duration`

rate-limits.note: No rate limit for a queue or a key. The README suggests a queue with fewer workers for throttling.
rate-limits.evidence: For throttling purposes, where you plan to have `limit` significantly larger than 1, we encourage relying on a limited number of workers per queue instead.

checkpoints.note: Active Job Continuations skip completed steps. They save progress before an isolated step, when the worker stops, or when a step raises an error.
checkpoints.evidence: When interrupted, the job will automatically retry with the progress serialized in the job data under the +continuation+ key. ... You can specify that a step should always run in its own execution by passing the +isolated: true+ option. ... it ensures that progress is serialized back into the job data before the step starts. (L170-L174: progress is also kept when a job raises an error after it has made progress.)

durable-waits.note: No signal wait. Before an isolated step, a continuation ends its run and resumes after the resume_options delay of its job class.
durable-waits.evidence: You can specify that a step should always run in its own execution by passing the +isolated: true+ option. ... :resume_options - Options to pass to +retry_job+ when resuming the job. Defaults to { wait: 5.seconds }. (continuable.rb#L94: retry_job(**self.resume_options). Looked at the Solid Queue README: no API makes a running job wait for a signal.)

dashboard.note: Mission Control – Jobs is a free separate gem from the Rails organization.
dashboard.evidence: "This gem provides a Rails-based frontend to Active Job adapters. It currently supports Resque and Solid Queue." ... "inspect and retry or discard failed jobs."

dead-letters.note: Failed jobs stay as failed executions. Retry or discard them from the console or Mission Control.
dead-letters.evidence: Jobs that fail will be kept in the system, and a failed execution ... will be created for these. The job will stay there until manually discarded or re-enqueued. ... failed_execution.retry # This will re-enqueue the job

queue-pause.note: A pause is a row in the database, so all workers obey it.

transactional-enqueue.note: The application starts an invocation with an HTTP request to the Restate Server, outside its database transaction.

debounce-throttle.note: An idempotency key returns the first response for a retention period, by default 24 hours. Throttling is planned. No option gives debounce.
debounce-throttle.evidence: Planned follow-ups include throttling and rate limits, invocation priorities, and finite queue (backlog) limits. docs/services/invocation/http.mdx#L100-L111: "If you re-invoke the service with the same idempotency key within 24 hours, Restate sends back the same response and doesn't re-execute the request to the service."

retries.note: Exponential backoff. By default, Restate pauses the invocation after the last attempt.
retries.evidence: "The retry policy always uses exponential back-off. You can tune the initial interval, the exponentiation factor and the maximum interval." Default: max-attempts = 70, on-max-attempts = "pause".

crash-recovery.note: The server retries the invocation on another instance and replays its journal.
crash-recovery.evidence: "If your function crashes or fails, Restate replays the journal, skipping completed steps"; "Service crashes or restarts: Any ongoing executions are retried on new instances."

cancellation.note: Cancellation is cooperative. The handler gets a terminal error at its next await point.

L119-L121: "A concurrency limit always applies **per scope**, never globally". release-notes/v1.8.0.md#L48: VQueues "are now on for every cluster".

rate-limits.note: No built-in rate limit. A documented recipe builds a token bucket in a Virtual Object.
rate-limits.evidence: "Built-in rate limits are planned as a follow-up. The token-bucket recipe below remains the way to do rate limiting today." "Restate doesn't have built-in rate limiting functionality".

checkpoints.note: The server records each step in a journal. A retry replays it and skips completed steps.

products.summary: Trigger.dev is an open-source platform for building AI workflows and long-running tasks in TypeScript, with retries, queues, observability and elastic scaling.

priorities.note: A priority is a time offset in seconds. A run with priority 10 starts before runs with no priority that were triggered up to 10 seconds earlier.
priorities.evidence: "The value for priority is a time offset in seconds that determines the order of dequeuing." "If you specify a priority of 10 the run will dequeue before runs that were triggered with no priority 8 seconds ago".

enqueue-deduplication.evidence: "If you trigger a task with the same idempotencyKey twice, the second request does not create a new run. It returns the original run's handle". L319: "By default idempotency keys are stored for 30 days."

debounce-throttle.note: The debounce option moves a delayed run later for each key. An idempotency key with a TTL gives one run for each key in a period.
debounce-throttle.evidence: When a run with the same debounce key already exists in the delayed state, subsequent triggers "push" the existing run's execution time later rather than creating new runs. docs/idempotency.mdx#L309-L315: "During this window, any subsequent triggers with the same idempotency key will return the original task run instead of creating a new one."

task-dependencies.note: A parent run waits for child runs with batchTriggerAndWait(), then starts the next task.
task-dependencies.evidence: "yourTask.batchTriggerAndWait(): Triggers a task multiple times in parallel and then waits until they're all complete. You get the resulting data to continue with."

retries.note: Exponential backoff with a factor, a minimum and a maximum delay, and optional randomization.
retries.evidence: retry: { maxAttempts: 10, factor: 1.8, minTimeoutInMs: 500, maxTimeoutInMs: 30_000, randomize: false }. errors-retrying.mdx: "You can configure retrying in two ways" (config file defaults or each task).

cancellation.evidence: "When a run is canceled: The task execution is stopped; The run is marked as canceled; The task will not be retried; Any in-progress child runs are also canceled". tasks/overview.mdx L557: "Signal will be aborted when the task is cancelled".
